newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia wage promises may be too good to be true.
newsitem.headline: Russia wage promises may be too good to be true.

text.p: New Russian government promises to pay billions of dollars in back wages may prove very difficult to fulfil, analysts said on Tuesday.
Government commitments made recently add up to a promise to pay about 26 trillion roubles ($4.50 billion) in wage arrears before mid-1998.

Sergei Kalashnikov, chairman of the State Duma lower house of parliament social and labour policy committee, said the government planned to pay in July military wages amounting to about half the 30 trillion roubles owed the sector.
The state has also promised to pay wages to other municipal servants by mid-1998, wages which the State Statistics Committee said in early June amounted to 11 trillion roubles.
Companies' wage debt was 43 trillion roubles and the state owed money to many of the companies.
Kalashnikov said collecting tax arrears would allow the government to meet its obligations to the military.
"Strengthening sanctions against budget debtors will do it," he told Reuters. "Total tax arrears are extremely high."
Unpaid wages and pensions anger millions of Russians while endless non-payments between companies strangle the economy.

Anton Siluanov, head of the Finance Ministry's Macroeconomic Department, said the state had paid 22 trillion roubles in pension arrears using proceeds from a $2 billion Eurobond in June, from domestic paper sales and from tax arrears paid up last week by gas group Gazprom.
The natural gas monopoly, the largest consolidated tax debtor, paid 14.5 trillion roubles in overdue taxes after many months of dispute with the government.

But this leaves the government with fewer taxes to collect and although it has had some success recently, it has a poor record of getting the overdue payments. It has threatened chronic non-payers with bankruptcy many times, but no major company has so far gone bankrupt because of failing to pay its taxes.
"Wage arrears are impossible to repay, they are too big," Kalashnikov said, adding the government would build up new debts as it paid off wages owed to soldiers.

Russia's national power utility Unified Energy System (UES) owes 396 billion roubles in back taxes, Yuganskneftegaz oil company owes 2.89 trillion roubles and AvtoVAZ car-maker owes 2.81 trillion roubles.
"I am afraid all the debts will never be repaid," said Dmitry Nikologorsky, an analyst with an independent Expert Institute.
